Every does_not_know term is given before use: APP fraud (Threat Model ¶1), money mules and the identity graph (scene ¶3), perceptual hash and its limits (scene ¶3, Fraud Signals ¶5), actor-level scoring (Architecture ¶9), friction economics (Step-Up Friction ¶5-6), point-in-time correctness and backtest/shadow/rollout (Architecture ¶4, ¶6), Verification of Payee (Banks ¶1). Terms flow readers met as unexplained (IBAN, "the gate", the Essen Golf, Sigma/Radar/Mercari in a preview list, callout use of "step-up friction") are familiar to the declared audience, previewed with a gloss, or part of the book's known context; none blocks understanding.

Opens with a direct-statement hook ("A listing marketplace is a machine for getting strangers to trust each other..."), then the chapter's terms, its place in the book and a roadmap; not a placeholder, restated question, dictionary definition, "dawn of man" or book report.

No "in conclusion"; the synthesis combines the sections into one answer and the second paragraph is the declared hand-off, not a new subtopic; no new evidence; does not end on a rephrased thesis alone.

States what no single section states, how graph, score, friction and labels combine to make the setup visible, and why it matters: it "moves the time from first fraudulent listing to cluster takedown from days to hours" and keeps the platform's trust from being borrowed.
Returns to Ingrid's day-one question ("Ingrid's day-one question now has one answer") and to the opening image of the trust strangers place in the platform being borrowed by fraudsters.

The intro reader names the off-platform nature of the fraud, the three owned terms, and the order Barcelona; threat model and verticals; signals; risk scoring service (real-time and batch, rules and models, actor scoring); step-up friction with cost-model thresholds; messaging; labels and adaptation; banks and police; back to Barcelona; trade-offs, failure modes, Chief Architect's view, questions. Evidence: UK Finance, OLX, Which?, Meta, Stripe, Airbnb and the fictional Veldmark. Matches expected.

The reader names every expected element: photo match with an unrelated, non-agency seller sent to fraud scoring, not duplicates; one listing score combining photo reuse, price, account age and verification; identity graph linking the accounts through the shared device at creation, cluster risk raising every member; one case for the cluster; remaining listings held at the gate that evening; a combined rule written and shadow-tested in hours.

The reader chooses the threshold by minimizing the explicit weekly cost (unstopped fraud x harm + genuine lost x value), lists fraud volume, share stopped, genuine abandonment and the two costs, assigns the cost of a lost genuine user to the marketplace general manager, abandonment to experiment, and says the threshold is revisited when fraud adapts. Matches expected.
